label: paragraph_title
text: THE FIRST STAGE.

label: text
text: For Ocean-Going Vessels to Discharge.

label: text
text: Financed by a Chinese millionaire, with the work carried out by the Netherlands Harbour Works Co., and supervised by the Port Development Department, the first and most difficult stage of one of the biggest schemes of private enterprise for harbour improvement yet put in hand is nearing completion.

label: text
text: This is the work at North Point, consisting of reclamation from the sea extending from the corner of the Electric Light Works to immediately below the Ming Yuen Gardens and the construction of a very fine quay wall providing ocean-going steamers and liners with 1,693 feet of berthage alongside without the necessity of wharves.

label: text
text: When the whole scheme is complete there will be godowns for the storing of cargo, these being within practically a sweep of the crane from the ship's hold, and the construction of the hundred foot road which is planned by the Government in that neighbourhood will materially help in the matter of transport. Thus, for the first time, will be large vessels be able to discharge on the Hongkong side and wasteful handling and re-shipment across the harbour will be eliminated.

label: text
text: The construction of the quay wall was one of the biggest schemes in connection with the undertaking, the contract for its construction being in the neighbourhood of $2,000,000 (or $1,050 per lineal foot. About seven eights of this wall is now completed. Rising from its foundations below the sea, it will allow of vessels drawing 30 feet to come alongside even at low water.

label: paragraph_title
text: 60 Ton Blocks.

label: text
text: The reinforced concrete blocks which have been used in the construction of the sea wall range in weight up to 60 tons. Some 1600 will have been used when the wall is finally completed, at a cost of $1,000 each. The huge moulds into which the concrete is poured provide for grooves and juggles in the respective adjacent blocks this providing an excellent adjusting medium for any subsidence in the rubble mounds which the wall has as a foundation.

label: text
text: An opportunity of inspection of the work of construction of the blocks, their transfer from the yard to the sea and their placement in exact alignment was afforded a "China" Mail representative yesterday through the courtesy of Mr. A. Anderson, Deputy Port Engineer. The greater number of the blocks have been made in the yard of the Netherlands Harbour Works, the demolition of the site of the old battery just behind having provided much of the material. As the work of block construction is now practically complete, the towering structure, which cannot fail to have attracted the attention of passers on the Shaukiwan Road has now been removed, and many of the Chinese brought from the North especially for the work have left. The quarry, too, is being filled in. The few blocks which remain to be done are now made on the opposite side of the road, nearer the Electric Light works.

label: text
text: Three 60 ton cranes are used for the removal of the blocks to trucks of tremendous strength, their transfer to barges and eventual placement on the scene of the work in the sea. The exact alignment of the wall here is somewhat of a wonder to any but the experts. It rises out of the sea just as if it had been built with all the conveniances of surface construction. Divers have, of course, worked in conjunction with surface workers in this connection.

label: paragraph_title
text: Rising From Sea.

label: text
text: Prior to the construction of the wall itself, some 200,000 cubic yards of sea surface had to be dredged, a sand trench made and the rubble mound foundation built, finer material gunged to an exact level providing the final top on which the concrete blocks rest. In the dredging, what is believed to be the second biggest dredger in the world was engaged, its ladder still being alongside the reclamation and giving an idea of its enormous capacity. Dredging was carried out over some portions to a depth of 90 feet.

label: text
text: As a fitting finale to his visit, the "China Mail" representative was allowed to make an underwater inspection of the wall's depth and construction by descending in diver's costume to the sea bottom, some 36 feet. The experience was a novel one and attendant with non-unpleasant feelings other than seemingly miniature explosions of the car at a depth below, twelve feet, and feeling of nervousness which is experienced when the screwing in of the mouthpiece as the final act on descending the ladder completely cuts one off from the upper world, a slightly sickly odour of rubber when one is thus encased and the sound of the escape of air which follows the screwing in of the mouthpiece.

A report from Canton details alleged plans to assist the Canton Government Aeronautical Bureau.
Inter alia, the intelligence is that there are nine "fighting 'planes, fitted with bomb devices, machine guns, &c. which will be shipped down from 'ladivostok, on instructions from Moscow." The report also says that there are sixteen expert Russian airmen in the Canton air service at present, the "crack" flying-men getting Gold $200 pay a month each. They are all paid by the Soviet continues the report, although performing so-called volunteer duties in Canton. The new aeroplanes are expected in a few months.

When the North Point scheme was first notified by Mr. A. G. M. Fletcher, he said that the Chinese business man who was behind it was so convinced of its possibilities that he had offered to undertake the whole of the work and to put up $10,000,000 for the purpose. He assured the Government that he could attract the flour and rice and general trade of West Point to that area; that if the Chinese had the facilities he had in view they would be prepared to move.

label: text
text:
In explaining his scheme of port development, Mr. John Duncan, Port Engineer, before he left for home, made mention of the scheme at North Point (possible extensions to which were included in his designs). It would have the advantage, he said, in contradistinction to development on the Kowloon side, of establishing competition in modes of transport. He believed that transport by junk would prove the cheaper but the existence of motor traffic would tend to keep down the charges for junks. The fact that Chinese merchants had their offices on the Hongkong side was another reason for extending accommodation for the staples of Chinese trade on the Hongkong side of the harbour, and reserving Kowloon for general cargo as at present.

label: text
text:
Hull, May 9.
Two constables and 17 civilians were admitted to hospital and 16 arrests made in Hull yesterday when the rioters damaged the trams and buses.
Police charges against the mob continued until midnight.

label: text
text:
The greatest asonishment and enthusiasm were aroused everywhere along the route yesterday by a convoy of 104 lorries laden with flour, with an escort of sixteen armoured cars, cavalry, and mounted police extending about two miles, which marched from the London Docks to Hyde Park whence the contents of the lorries were distributed to the district where the supplies were very short.
Two battalions of guards and 500 volunteers were sent down to the docks on Friday and helped to load the lorries yesterday morning.
Large crowds cheered the convoy, the sight being as popular as the Lord Mayor's procession.
A Good Spirit.
The spirit prevailing throughout the country was exemplified at Plymouth yesterday when a football match was played between a team of strikers and a team of police, the former winning by two goals to 1. The wife of the Chief Constable kicked off.
No Acceptance Yet.
London, May 9.
Reuter learns that the week-end did not produce any approach to the Government by the Trades Union Council in the direction of acceptance of the Government's decision regarding calling off the general strike before the negotiations are resumed.
